questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between Git and GitHub?

options.text: They are two names for the same program
Git is a version-control tool on your computer; GitHub is a service that hosts Git repositories
Git cannot run unless you have a GitHub account
GitHub is the command line and Git is the website

questions.explanation: Git is the open-source version-control tool that runs locally, with no account or internet required. GitHub is one online service that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features on top.

questions.prompt: In a distributed version-control system, what does each clone contain?

options.text: Only the latest version of the files
Only the changes you personally made
A full copy of the repository, including its entire history
A link to the server where the history is stored

questions.explanation: The defining feature of a distributed VCS like Git is that every clone mirrors the whole repository and its full history — which is why each clone is also a complete backup and works offline.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about Git are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Git stores each commit as a snapshot of the project
You can make a commit without an internet connection
Git was created for Linux-kernel development
Git requires a GitHub account to work

questions.explanation: Git stores snapshots (not diffs), works locally so you can commit offline, and was built by Linus Torvalds and the Linux community in 2005. It does not need GitHub — GitHub is just one place to host Git repos.

questions.prompt: The kind of version-control system in which every clone holds the entire history is called a ______ version-control system. (one word)
questions.explanation: Distributed version control (Git, Mercurial) gives every clone the full history, unlike centralized systems that keep history on a single server.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, 'GitHub is down, so we can't commit any code right now.' Why is this a misconception?

options.text: Committing is a local Git operation; you only need the network to push or pull
Commits are written directly to GitHub's servers as you type
You can commit, but only after switching to Subversion

questions.explanation: Because Git is distributed, the full repository lives on each machine. Committing, branching, and viewing history are all local — a GitHub outage only blocks syncing (push/pull), not committing.

questions.prompt: Match each system to its category.
questions.explanation: RCS is the classic local system; Subversion is centralized; Git is distributed; GitHub is not a VCS at all — it is a service that hosts Git repositories.
